questions.text: The job payload holds the token encrypted with an application key. Who decrypts it, and how does the worker turn it into the link in the email?
Where does the email link come from? What base URL and path does the worker build, and does it contain the raw token as ?t=TOKEN?
questions.about: Email worker -> Mail provider / Link handling

questions.text: What does the 'dummy hash' do in the unknown-address branch? Is it meant to match the time of the success branch, which does not hash a password?
questions.about: Notes: unknown-address branch should spend similar time

questions.text: The request flow says a new token revokes old unused tokens. If the user has a still-valid older link and then requests a new one, which link works and what does the older link show?
questions.about: UPDATE old unused tokens SET revoked_at

questions.text: In the submit flow, step 1 checks the password before BEGIN. If the token is already expired, does the user find out only after typing a valid password? What happens to the typed password?
After the reset the user is redirected to /login with no session cookie. Why is nobody logged in automatically, and what does the user do next?
The worker re-checks the token before sending. What does it check, against what state, and what does it do on a 'superseded' job versus a transient send error?
questions.about: Newer link issued / Email worker 3 retries, then log and drop

questions.text: What do 'sessions' hold, and how does the API use them for each request? What is the 'session cache in API (if any)'?

answers.text: The worker decrypts token_ciphertext with the same application key the API used to encrypt it. It builds the link from the configured base URL and the token, sends the email, then deletes the job. Sections 5 and 6 now say this. The encrypted token stays in the job because the token row, the revoke and the rate-limit count happen in the request transaction, so the request path stays self-contained.

The link is {PUBLIC_BASE_URL}/reset?t=<token>. The raw token appears only in that GET query string. The form then posts the token as a hidden field. The brief does not give the base URL value, so that value is configuration and I do not know it.

The dummy hash is removed. The success branch does not hash a password, so a dummy hash would not match its timing. The unknown branch writes nothing and the success branch writes two rows. We accept that gap for now and record it as open question 5, rather than add a fake cost. The brief asks only for the same message, not timing parity.

Only the newest link works. Revoked rows have revoked_at set. The page-load query requires revoked_at IS NULL, so an older link finds no row and shows the 'this link has expired, request a new one' page. Submit applies the same check under the lock. Checked against sections 3a and 3b.

Yes. The old order checked the password first, so the user could learn about expiry only after typing a valid password. Step 1 is now the token check, so an expired link shows the expired page before the password is checked. The typed password is held only in memory during the request. It is not stored or logged, and it is dropped when the expired page is shown. If the link expires during hashing, step 4 rejects it and the user sees the expired page.

The brief says not to log the user in automatically. The link proves control of the email, but signing in is a separate step, and it lets the user confirm the new password works. All sessions were deleted, including the device that did the reset. The user goes to /login and signs in with the email and new password.

Before sending, the worker reads the token row by token_id. It skips and deletes the job if the row is missing, revoked, used or expired. That is the superseded check. A skip is not retried. A transient send error uses the queue's existing 3 retries with backoff, then the job is dropped. Section 6 now states these rules.

A sessions row is one logged-in device. The API checks it on every request, as the brief says. The brief describes no session cache, so I do not know whether the API caches sessions. The design says to invalidate the cache on delete if one exists. This is open question 4.

questions.text: What does the worker do with a "password changed" job? Does it have a token_id or ciphertext, does the superseded check apply, and who gets the email?
What does normalising the email do here, and does it have to match how emails are stored in users?
What runs the 24 h purge of password_reset_tokens, and what does a user see if they click a link after its row was purged?
questions.about: Purge rows older than 24 h (5. Data)

questions.text: How does the worker claim a job from the queue, and what happens if the worker crashes after sending but before deleting the job?

answers.text: A password_changed job carries only kind and user_id, with no token. The worker reads the account's email address from users by user_id and sends the notice to that address. The superseded check does not apply, because there is no token to check. The same rule as reset jobs applies: up to 3 retries with backoff, then log and drop. Section 5 and section 6 now state this.

Normalising means trimming spaces and lower-casing the address, then looking it up. It must use the same rule as the login lookup, so one address always finds one account. I did not check the existing signup and login code. If that code uses a different rule, its rule wins and this line changes. Section 2 now states the rule.

A scheduled delete runs once an hour in the API, or as a cron job if the API has no scheduler. It removes token rows older than 24 h. The 24 h margin is well past the 30-minute link life and the 1-hour rate window. A user who clicks a link after its row is purged sees the expired page, the same as any unknown token, because the lookup finds no row. Queued jobs finish long before 24 h, so the purge never removes a row a job still needs. Section 5 now states this.

I do not know how the existing queue claims a job, such as by lease or visibility timeout, because the brief names the queue but not its claim rule, and I have not read its code. Decided part: if the worker crashes after sending and before deleting the job, the job may be sent again. This is accepted, because the resend carries the same single-use link and has no security effect. Section 6 and open question 7 now say this.

teachbacks.text:
1. Setup. Parts: a web client, an API server, Postgres (tables users, sessions, password_reset_tokens), an existing email queue, an email worker, and a mail provider.

2. The user asks for a reset. The client sends POST /password-reset/request with {email}. The API trims and lower-cases the email, using the same rule as the login lookup.

3. The API opens a transaction (BEGIN) and runs SELECT user FOR UPDATE. This locks that account, so concurrent requests for the same account are counted one after another. State is held in Postgres.

4. Branch: no user. The API skips to COMMIT and writes nothing.

5. Branch: user found. The API counts token rows created in the last hour. Superseded and revoked tokens count too. If the count is 3 or more, it skips to COMMIT and writes nothing.

6. Branch: fewer than 3. The API revokes the user's unused tokens. It generates a token (32 CSPRNG bytes, 43-character base64url) and inserts a row with only the SHA-256 hash, with expires_at set to created_at plus 30 minutes. It adds a `reset` job to the queue with {kind, token_id, user_id, token_ciphertext}. The ciphertext is the raw token encrypted with an application key. This is how the worker can later build the link without the raw token being stored in the table. All of this happens inside the transaction, then COMMIT.

7. Every branch returns the same 200 "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." The response does not wait for the email.

8. The worker claims the job from the queue. For a `reset` job it reads the token row by token_id. If the row is missing, revoked, used or expired, it skips and deletes the job, with no send and no retry. Otherwise it decrypts the ciphertext and builds the link `{PUBLIC_BASE_URL}/reset?t=<token>`. It sends through the mail provider. A send error is retried up to 3 times with backoff, then logged and dropped. In that case the user gets no email and no notice, and the token expires unused. The job is deleted when sent or dropped. Logs never contain the token or link.

9. The user clicks the link: GET /reset?t=TOKEN. The API computes sha256(TOKEN) and selects a token row with that hash where used_at and revoked_at are null and expires_at is in the future. If a row is found, it returns a 200 form with the token in a hidden field. If none is found, it returns a 200 "expired, request a new one" page. Loading does not consume the token. The response carries Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

10. The user submits: POST /reset {token, new_password}. The API repeats the token check. If it is invalid, it shows the expired page.

11. The API checks the password: at least 12 characters and not on a breached list. On failure it returns 422 with the form again. The token is untouched and still works until it expires.

12. The API hashes the password with argon2id before opening the transaction, so the lock is held only for the writes.

13. The API runs BEGIN, then SELECT the token row FOR UPDATE. If it is now invalid (for example, a double submit already used it), it does ROLLBACK and shows the expired page.

14. Still in the transaction, it updates users.password_hash, sets the token's used_at, revokes the user's other tokens, deletes all of the user's sessions, and adds a `password_changed` job. Then COMMIT. On a DB error it rolls back, and the password, token and sessions are unchanged.

15. The response is 303 to /login with no session cookie. The user then logs in with the new password.

16. The worker handles the `password_changed` job. It reads the email address from users by user_id and sends a "your password was changed" email. There is no superseded check. Retry and drop behaviour is the same as for reset jobs.

17. Cleanup. A scheduled job in the API runs hourly and deletes token rows older than 24 h. A link clicked after its row is purged shows the same expired page as any unknown token.

18. Known leftovers from the document: a crash after sending but before deleting the job may cause a duplicate email, which is accepted. A provider outage drops reset emails for every user. Dropped sends still use up the 3-per-hour quota.
gaps: Which CSPRNG, which application key and cipher, and where the key is stored are not stated. These only matter at the encrypt and decrypt steps.
How the worker claims a job is not stated. Open question 7 says the existing queue's lease or visibility rule is unknown, so I cannot say what happens to a claimed job if the worker dies.

Where the queue lives (inside Postgres or outside) is undecided (open question 3). That decides whether the 'add job' step in steps 6 and 14 is really atomic with the COMMIT, so I cannot say for certain whether a password_changed job is guaranteed to exist after a commit.
The breached-password source and refresh rule are undecided (open question 2), so I cannot say how step 11 actually decides that a password is breached.

The document does not say what the 303 or the success path shows the user about whether the reset worked. It also does not say how the user is told about a dropped email, which it says gets no notice.
